Reading

60 Minuten, 4 Teile mit steigender Schwierigkeit. Die Sektion mit dem grössten Zeitdruck der ganzen Prüfung. Faustregel: 12 bis 15 Minuten pro Teil, immer mit Stoppuhr üben.

Teil 1: Überschriften zuordnen

Langer Text in Abschnitten, pro Abschnitt die passende Überschrift wählen (mehr Optionen als Abschnitte).

Strategie: Hauptidee suchen, nicht Details. Erster und letzter Satz eines Absatzes tragen meist die Kernaussage. Falsche Überschriften greifen oft ein Detail auf, das nicht die Hauptidee ist.

Teil 2: Sätze in Lücken einsetzen

Entfernte Sätze an die richtige Stelle setzen. Testet Kohäsionsverständnis.

Strategie: Prüfe VOR und NACH der Lücke: Worauf zeigt this / they / such? Passt der Konnektor (however braucht einen Kontrast davor)? Passen Zeitformen?

Teil 3: Vier Autoren vergleichen

Vier kurze Texte zum gleichen Thema: Wer sagt was, wer stimmt überein, welche Nuancen trennen ähnliche Meinungen.

Strategie: Vor den Fragen pro Autor 3 Stichworte notieren (dafür/dagegen/neutral plus Hauptgrund). Dann Fragen gegen deine Notizen prüfen.

Teil 4: Langer Text, Multiple Choice

Inferenz, Ton, Autorabsicht, Synthese. Der schwierigste Teil.

Strategie: Falsche Optionen benutzen Wörter aus dem Text in falschem Zusammenhang. Nicht auf Wortgleichheit hereinfallen. Frage dich: Was MEINT der Autor, nicht was SCHREIBT er wörtlich.

Mini-Übung: Satz in die Lücke (wie Teil 2)

Signalwörter für die Textstruktur

FunktionSignalwörter
Kontrast folgthowever, nevertheless, whereas, on the contrary, that said, conversely
Ergänzung folgtmoreover, furthermore, in addition, what is more, likewise
Folge / Resultatconsequently, therefore, as a result, hence, thus, accordingly
Einschränkungnotwithstanding, despite, albeit, granted, admittedly
Autor-Meinungarguably, undoubtedly, it would seem, evidently, curiously

Tägliches Lesetraining

  • The Guardian oder BBC News: täglich 1 Artikel, danach in 2 englischen Sätzen zusammenfassen
  • The Economist: der Ton entspricht genau Teil 4 (Ironie, implizite Meinung, Inferenz)
  • Pro Artikel 5 neue Wörter notieren und aktiv in einem eigenen Satz verwenden
  • 1x pro Woche einen kompletten Reading-Teil mit 15-Minuten-Timer aus dem offiziellen Practice Book

Wie der Core deine Note beeinflusst

Das steht so im offiziellen Guide for Teachers und im Test Format Overview:

  • Jede Fertigkeit bekommt eine Zahl von 0 bis 50 und ein CEFR-Niveau.
  • Der Core (Grammar und Vocabulary) bekommt nur die Zahl, kein CEFR-Niveau.
  • Entscheidend: Wenn dein Ergebnis in einer Fertigkeit knapp unter einer CEFR-Schwelle liegt, wird deine Leistung im Core herangezogen, um das Niveau zuzuweisen.
  • Die Zahlen verschiedener Fertigkeiten sind nicht vergleichbar, weil die Schwellen je Fertigkeit anders liegen.
  • Ein Gesamt-CEFR-Niveau gibt es nur, wenn alle vier Fertigkeiten geprüft wurden.

Zwei Beispiele, was das konkret heisst:

FallWas passiert
A: Reading liegt knapp unter der C1-Schwelle, Core ist stark (zum Beispiel 44 von 50)Der starke Core spricht dafür, dass du die Struktur wirklich beherrschst. Er kann bei der Zuweisung zu deinen Gunsten den Ausschlag geben.
B: Gleiches Reading-Ergebnis, aber Core ist schwach (zum Beispiel 26 von 50)Es fehlt das Argument für die höhere Einstufung. Du bleibst auf dem tieferen Niveau, obwohl das Reading identisch war.

Praktische Folge für dich: Der Core ist die einzige Komponente, die auf alle anderen ausstrahlt. 25 Minuten, 50 Fragen, reines Wissen ohne Interpretationsspielraum. Das ist der Teil mit dem besten Verhältnis von Lernaufwand zu Wirkung, und genau darum liegt der Schwerpunkt dieses Portals dort.

Kleine Unstimmigkeit in den offiziellen Angaben: Die Webseite nennt für Speaking 12 Minuten, der Guide for Teachers 10 Minuten. Die Teilzeiten sind in beiden gleich (3 mal 45 Sekunden, dann 2 Minuten, dann 90 Sekunden und 45 Sekunden). Rechne mit rund 12 Minuten inklusive Anweisungen.

Was du wirklich brauchst: die offiziellen Cut Scores

Aus dem technischen Bericht des British Council (Aptis Scoring System, Anhang). Die Zahlen sind der Startpunkt des jeweiligen Niveaus auf der Skala 0 bis 50. Achtung: Das ist der Skalenwert, nicht die Anzahl richtiger Antworten.

Aptis AdvancedB1 abB2 abC1 abC2 ab
Listening14243850
Reading16284050
Writing22374450
Speaking22374450

Dein Ziel C1 heisst also konkret: 38 im Listening, 40 im Reading, 44 im Writing und 44 im Speaking. Writing und Speaking sind die Hürden, dort liegt C1 am höchsten. C2 gibt es nur mit der vollen Punktzahl 50.

Der Core hat keine Cut Scores, weil für ihn kein CEFR-Niveau vergeben wird. Er wirkt anders: Liegt dein Wert in einer Fertigkeit knapp unter einer Grenze, schaut das System auf den Core. Ist der stark, bekommst du laut Bericht "the benefit of the doubt" und wirst auf das höhere Niveau gehoben. Nach unten korrigiert der Core nie. Er kann dir also nur helfen.

Gesamtniveau: der gerundete Durchschnitt der vier Fertigkeitsniveaus. Du musst also nicht überall C1 haben. Beispiel aus dem Bericht: C1, C1, B2, B2 ergibt gerundet C1. Die Summe aus 200 Punkten ist davon unabhängig und sagt nichts über das Niveau.

Quelle: Aptis Scoring System, Technical Report v2.0, Anhang. Ein CEFR-Niveau wird nur vergeben, wenn du den Core mitschreibst.

Offizielle British-Council-Materialien (geprüft)

Das ist die wichtigste Quelle überhaupt: kostenlose Original-Übungstests mit Lösungsschlüsseln, direkt vom Prüfungsanbieter. Achtung: Die Übungstests zeigen kein Ergebnis, du musst dir deine Antworten notieren und danach mit dem Key vergleichen.

KomponenteÜbungstestLösungsschlüssel
Core (Grammar und Vocabulary)Test startenAnswer Key (PDF)
ReadingTest startenAnswer Key (PDF)
ListeningTest startenAnswer Key (PDF)
SpeakingTest startenBewertungsraster (PDF)
WritingTest startenBewertungsraster (PDF)

Dazu die beiden Handbücher: Test Format Overview und Guide for Teachers mit Beispielaufgaben zu jedem Teil.

Wichtig zur Punktzahl: Der Core wird von 0 bis 50 bewertet und bekommt kein eigenes CEFR-Niveau. Das Ergebnis wird benutzt, um dich in den anderen Komponenten richtig einzustufen. Ein guter Core-Wert hilft dir also indirekt überall.

Reading Advanced: das offizielle Format

60 Minuten für 25 Items in vier Teilen. Die Aufgaben starten auf B1 und werden von Teil zu Teil schwerer.

TeilAufgabeWichtig
1Opinion Matching: vier Meinungen, sieben Aussagen zuordnenDieselbe Person kann mehrfach die Lösung sein. Erst alle vier Texte lesen, dann Fragen, dann nochmals lesen. Auf Synonyme achten, nie auf gleiche Wörter.
2Long Text: langer Text (rund 750 Wörter), acht Überschriften für sieben AbsätzeEine Überschrift bleibt übrig. Zuerst den ganzen Text überfliegen, dann die Überschriften genau lesen.
3Global Understanding: Lückentext (rund 300 Wörter), fünf Lücken, je drei OptionenAlle Optionen sind grammatisch möglich. Nur wer den ganzen Text verstanden hat, trifft die richtige Wahl.
4Zwei Texte: sechs Lücken über beide Texte, je drei OptionenBeide Texte vor dem Antworten lesen, die Lösung hängt oft vom Zusammenhang zwischen den Texten ab.

Korrektur nach Abgleich mit dem offiziellen Answer Key: In Teil 3 und Teil 4 sind die Optionen im Advanced-Test ganze Phrasen, nicht einzelne Wörter (offizielle Lösungen sind zum Beispiel "highest living standards" oder "rule out"). Dafür gibt es neu Reading-Test I im echten Phrasenformat. Neu im Portal: Der Knopf unten startet einen kompletten Test mit allen vier Teilen hintereinander, 60 Minuten, ohne Zwischenlösungen. In Teil 2 siehst du dabei alle Überschriften auf einmal statt nur drei, genau wie in der echten Prüfung. Am Schluss kommt die volle Auswertung mit allen richtigen Antworten, dazu die Knöpfe für Fehler-Wiederholung und Lernblatt als PDF.

Formatangaben nach dem Überblick von Aptis Tutor und den offiziellen Beispielen des British Council. Die Texte und Fragen im Portal stammen aus deinem Buch und von mir.

Reading-Tests: 9 Tests mit je 4 Tasks (225 Fragen)

Aufgebaut wie im echten Test: Opinion Matching (7), Matching Headings (7), Single Text Gap-Fill (5), Multiple Text Gap-Fill (6), zusammen 25 Items in 60 Minuten. Tests A bis H stammen aus deinem Buch, Test I ist neu im offiziellen Phrasenformat von Teil 3 und 4. Alle Lösungen mit Textstellen-Beweis.

Reading-Test A (4 Tasks, 25 Fragen)
Task 1: Opinion Matching · Remote Work (7 Fragen, 10:00)
Person A: I must admit, the transition was jarring at first. I thrived on the buzz of the office. However, once I curated my home office space, my productivity skyrocketed. I do worry, though, that junior staff are missing out on the passive mentorship that happens simply by observing seniors in a physical room. Person B: For me, it has been nothing short of a liberation. The two hours I used to spend commuting are now invested in exercise and healthy meals. That said, I have noticed that management seems to be monitoring our online status more aggressively, which feels like a breach of trust. Person C: I view it as a double-edged sword. Practically, it makes sense. But psychologically it is isolating, and the boundaries between home and work have dissolved completely. I find myself answering emails at 9 PM. I honestly believe a hybrid model is the only sustainable future, otherwise burnout is inevitable. Person D: People complain about the isolation, but I have found it empowers me to be judged solely on my output rather than my office politics skills. My only grievance is the technology; when the server goes down, I feel completely helpless. It creates anxiety I never had when IT support was just down the hall.
FrageLösungWarum (mit Textstelle)
Who believes that remote work allows for fairer assessment of performance?Person DD: judged solely on my output rather than office politics. Paraphrase von fairer assessment.
Who is concerned about the lack of learning opportunities for less experienced employees?Person AA: junior staff missing out on passive mentorship. less experienced = junior.
Who feels that the company has become more intrusive?Person BB: management monitoring our online status more aggressively, a breach of trust.
Who struggles to separate their personal life from their professional duties?Person CC: boundaries between home and work have dissolved, emails at 9 PM.
Who misses the immediate availability of technical assistance?Person DD: IT support was just down the hall. immediate availability = direkt nebenan.
Who initially found the change difficult but now works more efficiently?Person AA: jarring at first ... productivity skyrocketed. Zwei Zeitstufen in einer Person, klassische Frage.
Who believes that a mix of office and home work is the best solution?Person CC: a hybrid model is the only sustainable future. mix = hybrid.
Task 2: Matching Headings · The Rise of Vertical Farming (7 Fragen, 12:00)
(1) By 2050, the global population is projected to exceed 9 billion. Vertical farming offers a radical alternative by moving agriculture into vertical layers, stacking crops in skyscrapers within city limits, producing far higher yields per square foot than traditional methods allow. (2) One of the most compelling arguments for this method is its independence from the climate. Traditional farmers are at the mercy of droughts, floods and unseasonal frosts. Vertical farms act as controlled environments where temperature, humidity and light are strictly regulated, ensuring year-round production. (3) This method also addresses resource waste. Traditional agriculture consumes a massive amount of the freshwater supply. Vertical farming uses hydroponic systems that recirculate water, using up to 95 per cent less water than field farming; nutrients are delivered directly to the roots. (4) Furthermore, the location of these farms revolutionises the supply chain. In the current model, produce travels thousands of miles, losing nutritional value and incurring a heavy carbon cost. By placing farms in urban centres, food miles are virtually eliminated. (5) However, the industry is not without critics, the primary concern being the reliance on artificial lighting. Simulating the sun requires vast arrays of LED lights, and the electricity required to power these facilities creates high operational costs. (6) Modern vertical farms are increasingly automated, using robotics to plant, monitor and harvest crops. Sensors collect data on every aspect of growth. This high-tech approach implies that the farmer of the future will need to be part botanist, part data scientist. (7) Despite the challenges, the potential for social impact is profound. Many urban areas are considered food deserts where fresh food is scarce. Repurposing abandoned buildings for vertical farming could give local communities access to healthy produce.
FrageLösungWarum (mit Textstelle)
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (1)?Maximising space in dense environmentsAbsatz 1: stacking crops in skyscrapers within city limits = Platz in dichten Staedten maximieren.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (2)?Protection from unpredictable weatherAbsatz 2: independence from the climate, droughts, floods, frosts = Schutz vor Wetter.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (3)?Water conservation techniquesAbsatz 3: 95 per cent less water, recirculate = Wassersparen.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (4)?Reducing the transportation footprintAbsatz 4: food miles virtually eliminated = Transportweg reduziert.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (5)?The high cost of energy consumptionAbsatz 5: LED lights, electricity, operational costs = Energiekosten.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (6)?The future of agricultural employmentAbsatz 6: part botanist, part data scientist = die Zukunft des Berufs. Falle: Der Absatz handelt von Technik, aber die HAUPTaussage ist der neue Beruf.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (7)?A solution to urban food desertsAbsatz 7: food deserts, access to healthy produce = Loesung fuer urbane Versorgungswuesten.
Task 3: Single Text Gap-Fill · Cognitive Dissonance (5 Fragen, 8:00)
Cognitive dissonance is a psychological theory that refers to the mental discomfort experienced by a person who holds two or more contradictory beliefs. This discomfort is triggered when a person's behaviour (1) ___ with their beliefs. For example, when people smoke and they know that smoking causes cancer, they are in a state of cognitive dissonance. To reduce this tension, humans are driven to find a resolution. This is often achieved by (2) ___ their thoughts or behaviours. A smoker might justify their habit by claiming that the research is inconclusive. This mental gymnastics is a defence mechanism designed to (3) ___ our self-image. Interestingly, this phenomenon is frequently exploited in marketing. Advertisers create a sense of dissonance by highlighting a gap between a consumer's current reality and their ideal self. The product is then presented as the (4) ___ to bridge that gap. Understanding this psychological trigger is (5) ___ for anyone studying human behaviour or persuasion.
FrageLösungWarum (mit Textstelle)
Luecke (1): ... is triggered when a person's behaviour (1) ___ with their beliefs. For example ...conflictsconflict WITH = im Widerspruch stehen. Buchloesung.
Luecke (2): ... resolution. This is often achieved by (2) ___ their thoughts or behaviours. A ...alteringaltering = veraendern. Man loest die Spannung, indem man Gedanken ANPASST, nicht bewahrt (preserving waere das Gegenteil).
Luecke (3): ... is a defence mechanism designed to (3) ___ our self-image. Interestingly, this phenomenon ...protectprotect our self-image = das Selbstbild schuetzen. Klangfalle detect/suspect!
Luecke (4): ... product is then presented as the (4) ___ to bridge that gap. Understanding ...remedyremedy = Heilmittel, Loesung. obstacle = Hindernis (Gegenteil), fallacy = Trugschluss.
Luecke (5): ... gap. Understanding this psychological trigger is (5) ___ for anyone studying human behaviour ...pivotalpivotal = entscheidend. Buchwort aus deiner Vokabelliste!
Task 4: Multiple Text Gap-Fill · Artificial Intelligence in Education (6 Fragen, 9:00)
TEXT 1: The integration of AI into the classroom is transforming education. Adaptive learning platforms analyse a student's performance in real-time, identifying weaknesses and tailoring the curriculum to (1) ___ their specific needs. Furthermore, AI can handle administrative tasks such as grading, freeing up teachers to focus on (2) ___ and mentorship. However, successful implementation relies heavily on unequal internet access, potentially (3) ___ the digital divide. TEXT 2: While the benefits are clear, there is significant skepticism. An AI might be able to teach calculus, but it cannot empathise with a student who is having a bad day. There is a fear that (4) ___ reliance on technology could lead to the de-skilling of the teaching profession. Moreover, if the algorithms are trained on biased data, they may inadvertently (5) ___ existing social inequalities. Therefore, educators insist that AI should be viewed as a tool to assist teachers, (6) ___ than a replacement for them.
FrageLösungWarum (mit Textstelle)
Luecke (1): ... weaknesses and tailoring the curriculum to (1) ___ their specific needs. Furthermore, AI ...suitsuit = passen zu. Buch-Key: B.
Luecke (2): ... freeing up teachers to focus on (2) ___ and mentorship. However, successful implementation ...pedagogypedagogy = Paedagogik, der menschliche Kern. Buch-Key: A.
Luecke (3): ... heavily on unequal internet access, potentially (3) ___ the digital divide. TEXT 2: ...wideningLogik: UNEQUAL access macht die Kluft GROESSER = widening. bridging waere das Gegenteil, die Hauptfalle! Buch-Key: C.
Luecke (4): ... day. There is a fear that (4) ___ reliance on technology could lead ...excessiveexcessive = uebermaessig. Nur zu VIEL Abhaengigkeit macht Angst. Buch-Key: A.
Luecke (5): ... on biased data, they may inadvertently (5) ___ existing social inequalities. Therefore, educators ...reinforcebiased data verSTAERKT Ungleichheit = reinforce. Buch-Key: B.
Luecke (6): ... as a tool to assist teachers, (6) ___ than a replacement for them ...ratherrather than = statt. Feste Wendung. Buch-Key: B.
Reading-Test B (4 Tasks, 25 Fragen)
Task 1: Opinion Matching · Space Tourism (7 Fragen, 10:00)
Person A: I think the commercialisation of space is an inevitable step in our evolution, but it feels like we are running before we can walk. We have not even sorted out the debris cluttering our own orbit, yet we are eager to send tourists up there. Until we have a sustainable framework for waste management in space, we should pause these vanity projects. It is about ensuring we do not turn the cosmos into another landfill. Person B: The price tag is obviously the biggest hurdle right now, making it an exclusive club for the ultra-wealthy. However, history shows that all technology starts this way. Remember early aviation? I believe that within two decades, a sub-orbital flight will be as affordable as a first-class plane ticket. The revenue from these early wealthy passengers is exactly what is funding the R&D to make it accessible for the rest of us. Person C: My concern is not the environment or the cost, but the safety protocols. We are relying on private companies who are essentially policing themselves. There is no unified international body regulating safety standards for space tourism. We need strict, enforceable government oversight immediately, rather than trusting the goodwill of tech billionaires. Person D: People are too focused on the logistics and missing the philosophical shift. Seeing Earth from space changes you. If we can get enough influential people and leaders up there to experience that, it could fundamentally change how we treat our environment back on Earth. The cultural impact will be worth every penny.
FrageLösungWarum (mit Textstelle)
Who believes that current regulations are insufficient?Person CC: no unified international body regulating safety standards.
Who compares space tourism to a historical transportation development?Person BB: Remember early aviation? Historischer Vergleich.
Who worries about the pollution caused by space activity?Person AA: debris cluttering our orbit, another landfill.
Who believes the experience could lead to positive behavioural changes on Earth?Person DD: change how we treat our environment back on Earth.
Who thinks the high cost is a temporary and necessary phase?Person BB: funding the R&D to make it accessible. Der hohe Preis finanziert die Zukunft.
Who advocates for a temporary halt to these activities?Person AA: we should pause these vanity projects. halt = pause.
Who suggests that private companies cannot be trusted to regulate themselves?Person CC: policing themselves ... rather than trusting the goodwill of tech billionaires.
Task 2: Matching Headings · The White Gold: A History of Salt (7 Fragen, 12:00)
(1) Long before it was a cheap seasoning, salt was one of the most sought-after commodities in history. In a world without refrigeration, salt was the only reliable way to preserve food for the winter or long journeys. This utility allowed civilisations to expand beyond their immediate food sources. (2) Because it was so essential, salt became a foundation for early economies. In Ancient Rome, soldiers were sometimes paid in salt, which is the origin of the word salary (from the Latin solarium). It was a medium of exchange functioning much like gold does today. (3) The demand for this mineral dictated the map of the ancient world. Great paths were worn into the earth to transport it, eventually becoming roads. The Via Salaria in Italy is one famous example. Cities like Salzburg grew wealthy solely by taxing the salt trade that flowed through their gates. (4) However, the value of salt also made it a tool of oppression. Governments realised that by monopolising salt, they could tax the population at will. The most famous example is the Salt March of 1930, led by Mahatma Gandhi, a simple act that galvanised the independence movement. (5) Today, the status of salt has shifted dramatically. With the advent of refrigeration, the need for salting food plummeted. Modern mining revealed that salt is actually incredibly abundant. As supply skyrocketed, the price crashed. What was once white gold became one of the cheapest substances on earth. (6) Despite its loss of economic prestige, salt remains vital for reasons most people do not see. The vast majority is used in the chemical industry to produce chlorine and caustic soda, essential for making paper, textiles, soap and glass, and to de-ice roads in winter. (7) Culturally, however, salt retains a spiritual significance that money cannot buy. In Japan, sumo wrestlers throw salt into the ring to purify it before a match. In the Bible, the covenant of salt symbolises permanence.
FrageLösungWarum (mit Textstelle)
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (1)?Methods of preservation before refrigerationAbsatz 1: the only reliable way to preserve food = Konservierung vor dem Kuehlschrank.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (2)?Salt as a currency and salaryAbsatz 2: soldiers paid in salt, origin of salary = Waehrung und Lohn.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (3)?Establishing trade routes and citiesAbsatz 3: Via Salaria, Salzburg taxing the trade = Handelsrouten und Staedte.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (4)?A catalyst for revolution and conflictAbsatz 4: Salt March, galvanised the independence movement = Katalysator fuer Revolution.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (5)?The decline of salt's economic valueAbsatz 5: price crashed, cheapest substances = wirtschaftlicher Niedergang.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (6)?Industrial applications beyond foodAbsatz 6: chemical industry, chlorine, de-ice roads = industrielle Nutzung jenseits von Essen.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (7)?The role of salt in religious ritualsAbsatz 7: sumo, Bible, covenant = religioese Rituale. Die zwei Extra-Ueberschriften (Geologie, Gesundheit) kommen im Text NIE vor.
Task 3: Single Text Gap-Fill · Bioluminescence (5 Fragen, 8:00)
Bioluminescence is the production and emission of light by a living organism. It occurs in a wide range of marine animals, as well as some fungi and insects. The light is created by a chemical reaction that (1) ___ within the creature's body. While we often associate this phenomenon with fireflies, it is actually the ocean where bioluminescence is most (2) ___ . In the deep sea, where sunlight cannot penetrate, this ability is crucial for survival. Organisms use this light for various purposes. Some use it to lure prey, while others use it to (3) ___ predators. For example, the vampire squid ejects a cloud of glowing mucus to confuse its attackers. Interestingly, the colour of the light is almost always blue or green. This is because these wavelengths travel the (4) ___ through seawater. Red light, by contrast, is quickly absorbed, which is why many deep-sea creatures are red in colour; they are effectively invisible in their (5) ___ .
FrageLösungWarum (mit Textstelle)
Luecke (1): a chemical reaction that (1) ___ within the bodyoccursBuch-Key: C. originates braucht ueblicherweise from, develops meint Wachstum ueber Zeit; occurs passt zum Kontext chemische Reaktion.
Luecke (2): the ocean where bioluminescence is most (2) ___prevalentBuch-Key: A. prevalent ist die Standard-Collocation fuer am haeufigsten verbreitet.
Luecke (3): others use it to (3) ___ predatorsdistractBuch-Key: B. reject und dismiss passen nicht zu einem Raubtier; distract = ablenken (Tintenfisch-Schleim verwirrt).
Luecke (4): these wavelengths travel the (4) ___ through seawaterfurthestBuch-Key: C. Es geht um die zurueckgelegte Distanz: furthest.
Luecke (5): effectively invisible in their (5) ___habitatBuch-Key: A. habitat = Lebensraum, der Ort wo sie leben.
Task 4: Multiple Text Gap-Fill · Urban Gardening (6 Fragen, 9:00)
TEXT 1: The Rise of Green Roofs. Urban gardening has evolved from a hobby into a necessity for modern cities. One specific adaptation is the green roof, planting vegetation on the top of buildings. This practice provides insulation, reducing the need for air conditioning in summer and heating in winter. (1) ___ , it helps manage stormwater runoff. In heavy rains, concrete cities often flood because water has nowhere to go. Green roofs absorb this water, releasing it slowly. (2) ___ the clear environmental benefits, the installation costs remain high, which discourages many developers. However, city planners are beginning to offer tax incentives to (3) ___ this reluctance. TEXT 2: Community Plots. While green roofs focus on infrastructure, community gardens focus on people. These shared spaces allow residents to grow their own food, but their primary value is social. They act as third places where neighbours who might never otherwise meet come together. (4) ___ , they provide a crucial source of fresh produce in food deserts, urban areas where affordable, nutritious food is hard to find. Critics argue that these gardens are inefficient and cannot (5) ___ feed a city. While this is true, proponents argue that the goal is not total self-sufficiency, but rather education and community resilience. (6) ___ , the psychological benefit of connecting with nature in a concrete jungle cannot be overstated.
FrageLösungWarum (mit Textstelle)
Luecke (1): ___ , it helps manage stormwater runoffFurthermoreBuch-Key: B. Furthermore fuegt einen weiteren Vorteil hinzu (kein Kontrast).
Luecke (2): ___ the clear environmental benefits, the costs remain highDespiteBuch-Key: A. Despite + Nomengruppe (the clear environmental benefits). Although braeuchte einen ganzen Satz.
Luecke (3): tax incentives to (3) ___ this reluctancecounterBuch-Key: B. counter = der Zurueckhaltung entgegenwirken. ACHTUNG: Deine handschriftliche Loesung im Buch war avoid, laut Answer Key ist counter richtig. Man vermeidet keine Zurueckhaltung, man wirkt ihr entgegen.
Luecke (4): ___ , they provide fresh produce in food desertsAdditionallyBuch-Key: A. Additionally fuegt einen weiteren Nutzen an. ACHTUNG: Deine handschriftliche Loesung war Therefore, das waere eine Folge, hier kommt aber ein zusaetzlicher Punkt.
Luecke (5): cannot (5) ___ feed a cityrealisticallyBuch-Key: A. realistically passt zur Machbarkeit.
Luecke (6): ___ , the psychological benefit cannot be overstatedFinallyBuch-Key: B. Finally fuehrt den letzten Punkt einer Aufzaehlung ein. Falle: At last = endlich (Erleichterung).
Reading-Test C (4 Tasks, 25 Fragen)
Task 1: Opinion Matching · The Ethics of Museum Repatriation (7 Fragen, 10:00)
Person A: I firmly believe that cultural heritage belongs in its original context. These objects were often acquired through colonial coercion or outright theft, and keeping them in Western museums perpetuates a legacy of inequality. Repatriation is not just about returning an object; it is about restoring a piece of identity to a nation that was deliberately stripped of it. Modern museums in the originating countries are fully capable of housing and protecting them. Person B: While the history of acquisition is certainly problematic, we must consider the educational benefits of the current situation. Large, global museums in places like London and Paris attract millions of visitors from all over the world, providing unmatched accessibility. If we fragment these vast collections, we significantly limit the global public's ability to view this shared human history. Person C: The legal ambiguity is the main issue. In many cases, the original transaction, even if coercive, was technically legal under the laws of the time. Simply declaring everything acquired before a certain date stolen creates a legal quagmire that could bankrupt institutions. I think a more pragmatic solution is long-term loans or shared ownership, allowing objects to rotate globally. Person D: The argument often ignores the safety and long-term security of the artefacts themselves. Many source countries lack the climate-controlled storage, security infrastructure and conservation expertise available in major Western museums. Returning priceless, fragile objects to potentially unstable regions could result in their degradation or loss, which is surely worse than keeping them safe abroad.
FrageLösungWarum (mit Textstelle)
Who focuses on the legal difficulties of determining past ownership?Person CC: legal ambiguity, technically legal, legal quagmire.
Who believes that keeping artefacts centralised maximises their educational reach?Person BB: millions of visitors, unmatched accessibility.
Who argues that the primary motive for repatriation is correcting historical injustice?Person AA: colonial coercion, restoring identity, legacy of inequality.
Who suggests a compromise involving rotating the objects rather than permanent transfer?Person CC: long-term loans or shared ownership, rotate globally.
Who is concerned about the physical condition of returned objects?Person DD: degradation or loss, lack of climate-controlled storage.
Who believes the originating countries are capable of caring for the objects?Person AA: fully capable of housing and protecting them. Direkter Widerspruch zu Person D!
Who worries that mass returns could financially ruin museums?Person CC: could bankrupt institutions.
Task 2: Matching Headings · Deep-Sea Hydrothermal Vents (7 Fragen, 12:00)
(1) Before the 1970s, scientists believed that life on Earth was entirely dependent on photosynthesis. The deep ocean floor was presumed to be a barren wasteland. In 1977, this paradigm was shattered with the discovery of hydrothermal vents in the Galapagos Rift, revealing vibrant ecosystems entirely divorced from the sun's energy. (2) These environments are created by seawater seeping down through cracks in the ocean floor near tectonically active zones. As the water encounters magma, it is heated to over 400 degrees. This superheated water dissolves minerals and jets back into the ocean, creating the characteristic black smoke plumes as minerals precipitate. (3) The temperature difference between the vent water and the surrounding seawater is staggering. Unlike surface life, where food chains start with plants converting light, here bacteria convert hydrogen sulphide into energy through chemosynthesis, forming the base of an entirely independent food web. (4) Around the vents, life has adapted to conditions that would kill most organisms instantly: crushing pressure, total darkness and toxic chemicals. Giant tube worms, blind shrimp and heat-tolerant crabs thrive here, each with remarkable biological adaptations. (5) The mineral-rich chimneys themselves have attracted commercial attention. The precipitated deposits contain high concentrations of copper, zinc, gold and silver, and several companies are developing technology to mine these formations, raising serious ecological concerns. (6) The contrast with the sunlit world above could hardly be greater. While surface ecosystems fluctuate with seasons and weather, vent communities live in constant conditions, their existence tied not to the sun but to the planet's internal heat. (7) Perhaps most profoundly, these ecosystems have changed the search for life beyond Earth. If organisms can flourish without sunlight here, similar life might exist in the subsurface oceans of icy moons such as Europa, making the vents a natural laboratory for astrobiology.
FrageLösungWarum (mit Textstelle)
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (1)?Discovering an unexpected environmentAbsatz 1: paradigm shattered, discovery 1977 = unerwartete Entdeckung.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (2)?The mechanism of the vent's chimney structureAbsatz 2: superheated water, black smoke plumes = wie die Schlote entstehen.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (3)?The surprising foundation of lifeAbsatz 3: chemosynthesis forms the base of the food web = die ueberraschende Grundlage des Lebens. Hinweis zum Buch-Key: Dort steht fuer Absatz 3 die Ueberschrift H (contrast with surface ecosystems), die aber auch fuer Absatz 6 angegeben ist. Da jede Ueberschrift nur einmal passen kann, ist C (Grundlage des Lebens, chemosynthesis) hier die logische Loesung. Im echten Test also beide Kandidaten pruefen.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (4)?Life forms adapted to extreme conditionsAbsatz 4: tube worms, blind shrimp, adaptations = ans Extreme angepasste Lebensformen.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (5)?A source of unique mineral depositsAbsatz 5: copper, zinc, gold, mining = einzigartige Mineralvorkommen.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (6)?The contrast with surface ecosystemsAbsatz 6: contrast with the sunlit world = Kontrast zur Oberflaeche.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (7)?The crucial role in the search for alien lifeAbsatz 7: life beyond Earth, Europa, astrobiology = Suche nach ausserirdischem Leben.

Reading-Test D (4 Tasks, 25 Fragen)
Task 1: Opinion Matching · Artificial Intelligence in Creative Arts (7 Fragen, 10:00)
Person A: I think the resistance to AI art is misplaced. Creativity is, after all, the recombination of existing ideas. AI is simply a powerful tool that allows for that recombination to happen on a scale no human could ever manage. It democratises creation, allowing someone with no technical artistic skill to realise a visual idea. We should treat it as the ultimate brush or synthesiser, not as a replacement for the artist's intent. Person B: My main worry is the erosion of authenticity. The value of art often lies in the knowledge of the human struggle, the unique perspective, and the hours of labour behind it. If a piece of music or poetry can be generated in seconds based on a statistical analysis of past works, it lacks the soul and emotional depth that gives art meaning. It is merely a highly refined imitation. Person C: The problem is legal and financial. AI models are trained on millions of copyrighted works scraped from the internet without compensating the original artists. This is not just unethical; it is an intellectual property heist. Until there are robust laws ensuring fair payment and proper attribution to the human artists who supplied the source data, the entire industry is built on stolen foundations. Person D: The most exciting development is the potential for collaboration. AI should not be seen as an artist itself, but as a sparring partner. Imagine a composer being able to test a thousand variations on a theme instantly. It elevates the human artist's ability to focus on the narrative and emotional core, outsourcing the technical drudgery.
FrageLösungWarum (mit Textstelle)
Who believes that AI is simply a highly advanced instrument for human use?Person AA: the ultimate brush or synthesiser, a powerful tool.
Who thinks the speed and ease of AI creation devalues the resulting artwork?Person BB: generated in seconds ... lacks the soul. Schnelligkeit entwertet.
Who suggests that the core of AI art is based on an illegal act?Person CC: intellectual property heist, stolen foundations.
Who is concerned that the origin of the art will lack genuine human feeling?Person BB: erosion of authenticity, no soul and emotional depth.
Who sees AI as a partner rather than a creator?Person DD: not an artist itself, but a sparring partner.
Who argues that AI makes artistic creation accessible to everyone?Person AA: democratises creation, no technical skill needed.
Who demands new laws before the technology can be considered legitimate?Person CC: Until there are robust laws ensuring fair payment.
Task 2: Matching Headings · The Legend of Atlantis (7 Fragen, 12:00)
(1) The story begins with Plato, who described a mighty island empire beyond the Pillars of Hercules. The empire was said to have succumbed to the hubris of its people and was consumed by the sea in a single day and night of disaster. (2) It is critical to note that Plato was not a historian; he used stories to illustrate his moral and political theories. Scholars generally agree that the tale of Atlantis served as a cautionary parable about the dangers of imperial ambition and spiritual decline, providing a stark contrast to Plato's ideal society. (3) However, the evocative nature of the story has consistently fuelled actual scientific and archaeological inquiries. The earliest major theory linked the legend to the massive Minoan eruption around 1600 BCE. This volcano on the island of Thera devastated the Minoan civilisation, and its cataclysmic tidal waves fit the description of rapid destruction. (4) Modern geology has added weight to the Thera hypothesis. The Aegean region is highly seismically active, and researchers have identified numerous ancient underwater settlements that were clearly submerged by seismic activity. While these do not match the scale of Plato's description, they prove that significant land-submergence events did happen in the right geographical area. (5) Another major theory points to the possible location near the Strait of Gibraltar. Researchers studying the Azores-Gibraltar Fracture Zone suggest that massive tectonic shifts could have caused the kind of sudden subsidence described in the text. However, solid evidence of a large Bronze Age civilisation in that region remains entirely absent. (6) While most academics view the search as futile, the legend continues to capture public imagination, leading to countless speculative expeditions. These are often fuelled by questionable discoveries on the sea floor, sometimes involving naturally formed rocks or modern shipwrecks misinterpreted as Atlantean ruins. This persistent fascination underscores humanity's desire to believe in lost grandeur. (7) The quest to locate Atlantis often overshadows the search for other, verifiable submerged cities. For example, the city of Heracleion off the coast of Egypt was truly lost to the sea for centuries. Studying the real mechanisms that caused the demise of such places is proving far more scientifically revealing than chasing Plato's literary creation.
FrageLösungWarum (mit Textstelle)
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (1)?A civilisation destroyed by its own arroganceAbsatz 1: succumbed to the hubris of its people = zerstoert durch eigene Arroganz.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (2)?A moral lesson, not a historical recordAbsatz 2: cautionary parable, not a historian = moralische Lehre, kein Geschichtsbericht.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (3)?A volcanic eruption as the first serious theoryAbsatz 3: earliest major theory, Minoan eruption = der Vulkan als erste ernsthafte Theorie.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (4)?Geological support from underwater discoveriesAbsatz 4: Modern geology has added weight, underwater settlements = geologische Stuetzung.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (5)?A promising location without proofAbsatz 5: However, solid evidence remains entirely absent = vielversprechender Ort ohne Beweis.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (6)?The enduring appeal of a mythAbsatz 6: continues to capture public imagination, persistent fascination = der anhaltende Reiz des Mythos.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (7)?Real sunken cities as better research targetsAbsatz 7: Heracleion, far more scientifically revealing = echte versunkene Staedte sind ergiebiger.

Task 1: Opinion Matching · The Future of Universities (7 Fragen, 10:00)
Person A: The core problem is speed. Industries reinvent themselves every five years, while a typical degree syllabus takes a decade to change. Learning institutions need to adapt their content far faster to remain viable, offering short, stackable micro-credentials that professionals can update throughout their careers. If universities refuse to modernise, private providers will simply replace them. Person B: Everyone talks about content, but a university was never just a content-delivery machine. Person D: Frankly, the economics no longer add up. Task 2: Matching Headings · The Future of Commuting (7 Fragen, 12:00)
(1) Cities worldwide struggle to absorb ever-growing streams of daily travellers. Congested roads and crowded platforms are no longer a minor inconvenience; commuting time has become a decisive factor in where people choose to live and work, forcing planners to rethink long-standing approaches to mobility. (2) One increasingly popular response is massive investment in high-capacity public transit. New metro lines, express bus corridors and regional rail aim to reduce the number of private cars entering city centres. However, expanding networks through dense, built-up areas is slow, disruptive and extraordinarily expensive. (3) In parallel, shared mobility is reshaping short journeys. Car clubs, e-scooters and bike-sharing schemes offer flexible solutions for the so-called last mile, but they demand new infrastructure and clear regulations, and cities that ignored this at first are now scrambling to catch up. (4) Digital technology adds a further layer. Routing algorithms bundle passengers into shared rides, and commuters increasingly rely on real-time apps to combine train, bike and foot into one seamless trip. These alternative models also raise questions about data privacy and who controls the underlying infrastructure. (5) Environmental pressures contribute strongly to the shift. The electrification of buses and trains, supported by falling battery prices, promises quieter streets and cleaner air, and the link between everyday transport choices and climate targets is now openly discussed in public. (6) Another crucial lever has nothing to do with vehicles at all: time. Staggered office hours and hybrid working spread demand across the day, so the same tracks and roads can carry more people simply because not everyone travels at once. (7) Taken together, these trends suggest that the commute of the future will not be a single technology but a menu of options, stitched together by software and shaped as much by policy decisions as by engineering.
FrageLösungWarum (mit Textstelle)
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (1)?When travel time shapes where we liveAbsatz 1: commuting time has become a decisive factor in where people choose to live.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (2)?The high price of expanding traditional networksAbsatz 2: slow, disruptive and extraordinarily expensive = der Preis des Netzausbaus.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (3)?Flexible options for the final stretchAbsatz 3: last mile, flexible solutions = die letzte Etappe.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (4)?Software as the new travel companionAbsatz 4: routing algorithms, real-time apps = Software als Reisebegleiter.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (5)?Cleaner vehicles for cleaner airAbsatz 5: electrification, cleaner air = sauberere Fahrzeuge.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (6)?Spreading the rush hour across the dayAbsatz 6: staggered office hours spread demand = Stosszeit entzerren. Der Absatz handelt von ZEIT, nicht von Fahrzeugen!
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (7)?A mixture of solutions rather than one answerAbsatz 7: not a single technology but a menu of options = Mix statt Einzelloesung.

Task 2: Matching Headings · The Journey of Coffee (7 Fragen, 12:00)
(1) According to Ethiopian legend, the story begins with a goat herder named Kaldi, who noticed his animals becoming unusually energetic after eating red berries from a certain shrub. Whatever the truth of the tale, botanists agree that the coffee plant is native to the highlands of Ethiopia. (2) From Africa, the bean crossed the Red Sea to Yemen, where Sufi monasteries brewed it to stay awake during long nights of devotion. The port of Mocha became the centre of a jealously guarded trade, and for two centuries the Arab world held a near monopoly on cultivation. (3) The drink's stimulating effect soon attracted suspicion. Coffee was briefly banned by religious authorities who feared the coffee houses were fostering radical political thought and anti-government gossip. Similarly, King Charles II of England once attempted to shutter all coffee houses, labelling them nurseries of sedition and rebellion. (4) By the 17th century, the bean began its journey into Europe via Venice, which had extensive trade links with the Ottoman Empire. Initially marketed as a powerful medicine that aided digestion, it was in England, however, that the coffee house truly flourished as a social and intellectual phenomenon, swiftly replacing ale as the standard breakfast drink. (5) In London, these establishments were often dubbed penny universities: for the price of a penny, one could buy a cup of coffee and engage in conversation with academics, merchants and poets. Many influential businesses, including Lloyd's of London, initially a coffee shop, were founded and conducted their affairs in these venues. (6) Realising the vast commercial potential, European colonial powers sought to break the Arab monopoly on coffee production. They began smuggling fertile beans out of the Middle East. The Dutch were the first to succeed, establishing plantations in Java and Ceylon; this forced expansion marked coffee's transition to a major global agricultural export. (7) Today, the beverage is the second most traded commodity in the world after oil. Its widespread success is due entirely to the presence of caffeine, a psychoactive stimulant. Science has now confirmed its effects: it blocks adenosine, a neurotransmitter that makes us feel tired, acting as a short-term cognitive enhancer.
FrageLösungWarum (mit Textstelle)
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (1)?Legendary origins in the Ethiopian highlandsAbsatz 1: Kaldi-Legende, native to the highlands of Ethiopia = legendaerer Ursprung.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (2)?An early monopoly built on devotion and tradeAbsatz 2: Sufi monasteries, Mocha, near monopoly = Monopol aus Andacht und Handel.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (3)?Authorities alarmed by a new drinkAbsatz 3: banned by religious authorities, Charles II, sedition = alarmierte Obrigkeit. Woertlich aus deinem Buch (Seite 29).
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (4)?Arrival in Europe as medicine and social habitAbsatz 4: via Venice, marketed as medicine, replaced ale = Ankunft in Europa. Buchtext woertlich.

Task 1: Opinion Matching · The Privatisation of Public Services (7 Fragen, 10:00)
Person A: The primary argument for privatisation, efficiency, is often a red herring. While private firms may cut initial costs, they invariably do so by lowering standards, reducing staff pay and neglecting long-term maintenance. When something goes wrong, the taxpayer is often left to pick up the pieces, without the direct accountability that a publicly managed service would entail. It is simply a recipe for short-sighted financial decisions. Person B: I see it as the only sustainable route for essential services. Government departments are often slow, hampered by bureaucracy, and lack the specialist expertise and incentive for innovation found in the private sector. By allowing competition, you encourage efficiency and drive down prices for the consumer. Strict regulatory oversight is, of course, absolutely crucial to prevent profiteering, but the market mechanism itself is sound. Person C: My concern is the ethical dimension. Essential services like healthcare, prisons and utilities should never be managed for profit. When you introduce a financial motive to something like prison management, the incentive shifts from rehabilitation to maximising occupancy and minimising expenditure, which fundamentally undermines the social contract. There should be a clear line drawn; basic human needs must remain in public hands. Person D: The benefit is largely felt by the public purse. Selling off state-owned assets provides a much-needed windfall for the treasury, which can then be invested elsewhere, such as in education or infrastructure. Furthermore, private companies are much better placed to raise capital for large-scale investment projects without burdening the national debt. It is a method of injecting private sector dynamism into stale public institutions.

Who suggests that the core function of certain services should preclude a profit motive?Person CC: should never be managed for profit. preclude kennst du: ausschliessen!

Who focuses on the lack of transparency and accountability when problems arise?Person AA: without the direct accountability that a publicly managed service would entail.

Task 2: Matching Headings · The Science of Sleep (7 Fragen, 12:00)
(1) We spend roughly a third of our lives asleep, yet for most of history nobody could say why. Far from being a passive shutdown, sleep is now known to be an intensely active state in which the brain performs tasks that are impossible while we are awake. (2) Sleep unfolds in repeating cycles, alternating between deep slow-wave sleep and Rapid Eye Movement, or REM, sleep. During deep sleep, muscle activity drops, growth hormone increases and the body concentrates on physical repair, while REM is when most vivid dreaming occurs. (3) One of the most important functions of this nightly rhythm is memory consolidation. The sleeping brain replays the experiences of the day, strengthens the connections worth keeping and discards irrelevant details, turning fragile impressions into durable, long-term knowledge. (4) Dreams themselves may serve a purpose beyond entertainment. Some researchers propose that the brain uses them as a safe simulator, weaving recent worries into imagined scenarios; on this view, even nightmares have a logical basis, letting us rehearse threats without real danger. (5) Evolution also seems to have shaped sleep as a safety mechanism. By rendering early humans inactive during the dark, the most dangerous hours of the night, a time when hunting was impossible and predators were active, sleep reduced the risk of accident, injury or predation, effectively preserving energy while ensuring survival. (6) Another critical function, independent of physical rest, is the clearing of metabolic waste. During waking hours, brain cell activity generates toxic byproducts. Recent discoveries highlight the role of the glymphatic system, a network that actively flushes these toxins, including proteins associated with Alzheimer's, from the brain, and this cleansing is significantly more active during sleep. (7) Given all this, the consequences of chronic sleep deprivation are predictably severe: weakened immunity, impaired judgement, emotional instability and a measurably higher risk of long-term disease. Sleep, the research concludes, is not a luxury to be minimised but a biological necessity.
FrageLösungWarum (mit Textstelle)
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (1)?An active process, not a passive stateAbsatz 1: intensely active state, not a passive shutdown.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (2)?The two alternating stages of the nightAbsatz 2: deep slow-wave sleep und REM = die zwei Phasen. Buchbegriffe woertlich.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (3)?Turning daily experience into lasting memoryAbsatz 3: memory consolidation, discards irrelevant details, durable long-term = Erinnerung festigen. Buchtext.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (4)?A possible purpose for dreamingAbsatz 4: even nightmares have a logical basis, safe simulator = Zweck des Traeumens.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (5)?Staying safe by staying stillAbsatz 5: safety mechanism, inactive during the dark, predators = Sicherheit durch Stillhalten. Buchtext woertlich (Seite 26).
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (6)?The brain's nightly cleaning serviceAbsatz 6: glymphatic system flushes toxins, more active during sleep = naechtliche Reinigung. Buchtext woertlich.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (7)?The price of not sleeping enoughAbsatz 7: weakened immunity, impaired judgement = der Preis des Schlafmangels.

Reading-Test H (4 Tasks, 25 Fragen)
Task 1: Opinion Matching · Social Media and Political Discourse (7 Fragen, 10:00)
Person A: I see social media as an indispensable tool for accountability. It allows citizens to bypass traditional media gatekeepers and scrutinise politicians' actions directly and immediately. While it can be messy, the instant feedback loop forces leaders to address issues that might otherwise be ignored. The potential for grassroots movements to mobilise so quickly is a powerful, democratising force that shouldn't be underestimated. Person B: My main concern is the echo chamber effect. Algorithms prioritise content that confirms a user's existing beliefs, leading to a polarised environment where extreme views flourish and compromise becomes impossible. People are no longer debating facts; they are simply reinforcing tribal identities. It's creating a highly toxic, unproductive political landscape, and the speed at which misinformation spreads is terrifying. Person C: I believe the problem lies with the sheer lack of depth. Complex policy issues, like healthcare reform or economic trade, cannot be adequately discussed in a 280-character post or a viral video. The platforms reward sensationalism and superficial outrage, discouraging reasoned analysis and thoughtful deliberation. It's reducing serious political engagement to a form of entertainment, which does a huge disservice to the public. Person D: The most worrying aspect for me is the issue of anonymity and targeted interference. Foreign actors can easily create fake profiles and launch coordinated disinformation campaigns to influence elections in other countries. These platforms are effectively weaponised, operating without the kind of regulation that applies to television or print media. Until the responsibility for authenticating users is strictly enforced, these systems pose a serious national security threat.
FrageLösungWarum (mit Textstelle)
Who is primarily concerned with foreign interference in domestic affairs?Person DD: Foreign actors, disinformation campaigns, influence elections. Deine Buch-Annotation: D!
Who believes that the structure of the platforms discourages detailed discussion?Person CC: cannot be adequately discussed in a 280-character post. Deine Annotation: C, mit deiner Notiz adequately = ausreichend!
Who argues that the main benefit is holding public figures directly responsible?Person AA: accountability, scrutinise politicians actions directly. Annotation: A.
Who is worried that political discussion has become overly divisive and insular?Person BB: echo chamber, polarised, tribal identities. divisive = spaltend, insular = abgeschottet.
Who views the platforms as a positive force for organising public action quickly?Person AA: grassroots movements mobilise so quickly, democratising force. Annotation: A.
Who suggests that politics is being treated too lightly, like a leisure activity?Person CC: reducing serious political engagement to a form of entertainment.
Who focuses on the danger of unverified accounts spreading harmful stories?Person DD: anonymity, fake profiles, authenticating users. Annotation: D.
Task 2: Matching Headings · The Decline of the High Street (7 Fragen, 12:00)
(1) For centuries, the high street was the undisputed heart of town life: the place where people shopped, met, worked and celebrated. Its shops financed the upkeep of the centre, and its footfall sustained everything from cafes to public services around it. (2) That historical function has been eroded most visibly by the internet. Online retail offers wider choice, lower prices and doorstep delivery, and every year a larger share of spending migrates to platforms that never need a shopfront at all. (3) Even among physical stores, the centre is losing ground. Shoppers increasingly prefer larger retail parks on the edge of town, where parking is free, units are spacious and several major chains sit conveniently side by side. (4) Traders who remain in the centre face a punishing cost base. Commercial rents and business rates were set in a more prosperous era, and combined with delivery restrictions and expensive parking, they make many small shops financially unviable. (5) The businesses that do thrive tend to sell what cannot be posted: experiences. Cafes, barbers, gyms, galleries and street food markets draw people in for leisure, and analysts speak of a rise of experiential shopping replacing routine purchasing. (6) Local and national government have begun to respond with support initiatives: rate relief for independents, funds to convert empty units, and events designed to bring footfall back on evenings and weekends. (7) The most promising vision, however, goes further than retail. Planners increasingly argue that surplus shop space should become housing, clinics and workspaces, reinventing the centre as a place where people actually live rather than merely a place where they once shopped.
FrageLösungWarum (mit Textstelle)
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (1)?The historical function of the town centreAbsatz 1: the undisputed heart of town life = die historische Funktion. Buch-Ueberschrift woertlich (Seite 31).
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (2)?Spending moves to the online worldAbsatz 2: online retail, spending migrates = Verlagerung ins Netz.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (3)?The changing preference for larger retail parksAbsatz 3: larger retail parks on the edge of town = Praeferenz fuer Retail-Parks. Buch-Ueberschrift woertlich.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (4)?The burden of rents and business ratesAbsatz 4: rents and business rates, financially unviable = die Kostenlast.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (5)?The rise of leisure and experiential shoppingAbsatz 5: experiences, experiential shopping = Erlebnis statt Einkauf. Buch-Ueberschrift woertlich.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (6)?Government support initiativesAbsatz 6: rate relief, funds, events = staatliche Unterstuetzung. Buch-Ueberschrift woertlich.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (7)?Reinventing the centre as a place to liveAbsatz 7: housing, clinics, a place where people actually live = das Zentrum neu erfinden.

Task 1: Opinion Matching · Working from home permanently (7 Fragen, 10:00)

Person B: Our team has been remote for four years and productivity has never dipped. What has suffered is the training of new staff. You cannot learn a craft by watching a screen; you learn it by sitting next to someone and overhearing how they handle a difficult client. We are storing up a problem for the next generation. Person C: I went back to the office voluntarily after eight months. Working from my flat, I found that the day never really ended. The commute annoyed me for years, but it turns out that it was doing something useful: it told my brain the working day was over. Person D: The debate is far too focused on preference. Now we absorb it, and nobody has adjusted salaries to reflect it.

Task 2: Matching Headings · The return of the night train (7 Fragen, 12:00)
(1) For three decades the sleeper train looked like a museum piece. Budget airlines undercut it on price, high-speed lines beat it on daytime speed, and one operator after another quietly withdrew its carriages. (2) The reversal began not with the railways but with the passengers. As flying became harder to justify on environmental grounds, a generation of travellers started looking for an alternative that did not involve an airport at six in the morning. (3) Austria's national operator took the gamble that others would not, buying up abandoned rolling stock and rebuilding a network across the Alps. Within a few years its night services were carrying well over a million passengers annually. (4) The economics remain awkward. A sleeper carriage carries far fewer people than a seated one, staff must be paid through the night, and the train occupies expensive track while most of the country is asleep. (5) Track access charges are the hidden obstacle. Because each country prices its rails differently, a train crossing four borders pays four separate bills, and a single national increase can wipe out the margin on an entire route. (6) Comfort has been the main battleground for new entrants. Private cabins with proper beds, showers at the end of the corridor and a dining car that serves regional food are what convince travellers to pay more than an airline would charge. (7) Whether the revival lasts will depend less on nostalgia than on policy. Where governments have treated the night train as public infrastructure rather than a commercial curiosity, the services have survived their first difficult years.

Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (1)?Decades of declineAbsatz 1: looked like a museum piece, operators withdrew = Jahrzehnte des Niedergangs.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (2)?A change driven by travellersAbsatz 2: began not with the railways but with the passengers = die Reisenden treiben die Wende.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (3)?One operator takes the riskAbsatz 3: took the gamble that others would not = ein Betreiber wagt es.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (4)?Why the numbers rarely workAbsatz 4: far fewer people, staff paid through the night = die Rechnung geht kaum auf.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (5)?The problem of crossing bordersAbsatz 5: four separate bills = das Problem der Grenzen.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (6)?Competing on comfort, not priceAbsatz 6: private cabins, showers, dining car = Wettbewerb ueber Komfort.
Welche Ueberschrift passt zu Absatz (7)?The role of political decisionsAbsatz 7: depend less on nostalgia than on policy = politische Entscheidungen.

Listening

30 Minuten, 11 Aufgaben mit 11 Aufnahmen. Die meisten Aufnahmen kannst du zweimal hören. Getestet wird zunehmend Meinung und Haltung, nicht nur Fakten.

Listening Trainer mit Sprachausgabe

Lies zuerst Frage und Optionen, dann spiel die Aufnahme ab. Wie in der Prüfung darfst du jede Aufnahme höchstens zweimal hören. Nach der Antwort siehst du Erklärung und Transkript. Die Hörtexte sind selbst erstellt im Aptis Advanced Format, nicht aus dem Buch.

Tempo

So bekommst du die beste Stimme
  • iPhone und iPad: Einstellungen, Bedienungshilfen, Gesprochene Inhalte, Stimmen, Englisch (Grossbritannien). Eine Stimme mit "Premium" oder "Erweitert" laden, danach die Seite neu öffnen.
  • Mac: Systemeinstellungen, Bedienungshilfen, Gesprochene Inhalte, Systemstimme, Stimmen verwalten. Englisch (UK) Premium laden.
  • Windows: Microsoft Edge nutzen. Dort stehen die neuronalen "Natural" Stimmen ohne Installation bereit.
  • Android und Chrome: die Google UK English Stimmen sind vorinstalliert.

Transkript

Teil 1: Fünf kurze Aufnahmen

Monologe oder Dialoge, je 1 Frage. Detailverständnis: Zahlen, Orte, Absichten, Vereinbarungen.

Falle: Oft werden mehrere Zahlen oder Orte genannt, aber nur einer beantwortet die Frage. Höre auf Korrektursignale wie actually, on second thoughts, no wait.

Teil 2: Drei Monologe

Je 2 Fragen pro Aufnahme. Meinung, Begründung, Haltung des Sprechers.

Strategie: Achte auf Bewertungswörter: disappointing, remarkable, overrated, worthwhile. Sie verraten die Haltung schneller als der Inhalt.

Teil 3: Diskussion Mann / Frau

Aussagen auf dem Bildschirm zuordnen: Wer sagt was, worüber sind sich beide einig.

Falle: Erwähnen ist nicht zustimmen! Ein Sprecher kann eine Meinung nennen und sie dann ablehnen (Some people say X, but I find that hard to believe).

Universalstrategie

  • Fragen VOR der Aufnahme lesen, Schlüsselwörter markieren
  • Erstes Hören: Antwort wählen. Zweites Hören: nur bestätigen
  • Die richtige Antwort ist fast immer eine PARAPHRASE, nie die Wörter der Frage
  • Wenn du eine Aufnahme verpasst: sofort loslassen, die nächste zählt gleich viel

Paraphrasen erkennen (die wichtigste Listening-Fähigkeit)

Du hörst...Die Antwort sagt...
It cost far more than we expected.The price exceeded the budget.
I don't see the point of the new policy.She questions the value of the change.
We had to postpone the launch twice.The release was delayed repeatedly.
Hardly anyone turned up.Attendance was very low.

Tägliches Hörtraining

  • TED Talks: 1 Talk täglich, erst ohne, dann mit Untertiteln, danach 3 Kernaussagen laut auf Englisch wiedergeben
  • BBC Podcasts: The Global Story oder Business Daily für C1-Tempo
  • YouTube-Kanal von Aptis Tutor: Listening-Beispiele im exakten Prüfungsformat
  • Beim Pendeln nach Dübendorf: Podcast plus laute Zusammenfassung = Listening und Speaking gleichzeitig

Die vier Hörfallen und wie du sie knackst

FalleWas passiertDeine Gegenmassnahme
ParaphraseDie richtige Antwort benutzt fast nie die Wörter der Frage. Wer das gleiche Wort hört und sofort klickt, tappt meistens daneben.Frage vorher lesen und im Kopf umformulieren: Was hiesse das mit anderen Wörtern?
Korrektur mitten im SatzDer Sprecher nennt zuerst eine falsche Fährte und korrigiert sich dann.Signalwörter abwarten: Actually... / Well, to be honest... / On second thoughts... / Having said that... Was DANACH kommt, ist die Antwort.
Erwähnen ist nicht zustimmenIn Teil 3 nennt eine Person eine Meinung, nur um sie abzulehnen.Auf Verben achten: I doubt / I am not convinced / some people claim markieren fremde Meinungen.
Zahlen und NamenMehrere Zahlen werden genannt, nur eine beantwortet die Frage.Beim ersten Hören alle Zahlen kurz mitschreiben, beim zweiten nur noch zuordnen.

Ablauf, der immer funktioniert: Fragen VOR der Aufnahme lesen und Schlüsselwörter markieren, beim ersten Hören entscheiden, beim zweiten nur bestätigen. Nie während des Hörens noch an der vorherigen Frage hängen.

Tägliches Training: ein TED Talk pro Tag, erst ohne Untertitel. BBC 6 Minute English zum Aufwärmen, The Global Story für C1-Tempo. Beim Pendeln: Podcast hören und danach drei Kernaussagen laut auf Englisch wiederholen, das trainiert Hören und Sprechen gleichzeitig.

Writing

45 Minuten, genau 3 Teile. Bewertet werden Task Fulfilment und Register, Grammatical Range, Vocabulary Range und Cohesion. Unten findest du das komplette Format, Musterantworten und dann einen vollständigen Test mit KI-Korrektur direkt hier auf der Seite.

Das exakte Advanced-Format

TeilAufgabeUmfangZeitRegister
1Chat: 3 Nachrichten von Mitgliedern beantwortenje 30 bis 40 Wörterca. 10 Min.Informell: Kurzformen (I'm, don't), locker, persönlich
2E-Mail einer Behörde/Organisation beantworten, mit vorgegebenen Notizen, Gefühle ausdrücken120 bis 150 Wörterca. 15 Min.Streng formell: keine Kurzformen, höflich, indirekt
3Artikel für eine Online-Publikation, basierend auf Research Notes (oft mit Zahlen/Diagramm)180 bis 220 Wörterca. 20 Min.Sachlich, informativ UND interessant, klare Absätze

Wortzahl ist Pflicht: zu wenig kostet Punkte, alles über dem Limit wird nicht gewertet. Vor dem Weiterklicken immer Rechtschreibung und Zeichensetzung prüfen, zurück geht es nicht.

Informell vs. formell: die Übersetzungstabelle

Informell (Teil 1)Formell (Teil 2)
Hi / Hi thereDear Mr / Ms + Name, Dear Sir or Madam
I'm writing to answer your email.I am writing in response to your email.
Sorry, but I can't come.I am afraid I will be unable to attend.
Can you let me know...?I would be grateful if you could inform me...
becausedue to the fact that / owing to
Feel free to get in touch.Please do not hesitate to contact me.
Best / Cheers / See youYours sincerely (Name bekannt) / Yours faithfully (unbekannt)

Struktur E-Mail (Teil 2)

  • Anrede plus Bezug: I am writing in response to your email regarding...
  • Gefühl ausdrücken (steht fast immer in der Aufgabe!): I was disappointed to learn that... / I must express my concern about...
  • Alle Notizen-Punkte abarbeiten, je 1 bis 2 Sätze
  • Konstruktiver Vorschlag: I would suggest that... / One possible solution would be...
  • Schluss: I look forward to hearing from you.

Struktur Artikel (Teil 3)

  • Titel: kurz, neugierig machend
  • Einstieg: Leser abholen, gerne mit Frage (Have you ever wondered...?)
  • Hauptteil: Zahlen aus den Notes einbauen (rose from 8 to 34 percent, account for...)
  • Vor- und Nachteile abwägen
  • Schluss mit Ausblick: This trend is likely to continue... / Only time will tell whether...
